questions.stem: Why must genetic material be replicated before a cell divides?
options: So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the genetic information
So that each new cell receives half of the parent cell's genetic information
So that the parent cell can keep one copy and destroy the other copy
So that mutations can be added to the copy that passes to new cells
questions.explanation: Continuity of life depends on each daughter cell inheriting a full set of genetic instructions. Halving the genetic material happens only in meiosis, which forms gametes.

questions.stem: By which process do bacteria reproduce?
options: Binary fission
Mitosis
Meiosis
Fertilisation
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission, copying their circular chromosome and splitting into two cells. Mitosis and meiosis are divisions of the nucleus in eukaryotic cells, and bacteria have no nucleus.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes binary fission in a bacterium?
options: The chromosome is halved, the halves move to opposite ends, and the cell membrane fuses in the middle
Two cells fuse, their chromosomes pair up, and the combined cell then splits into four new cells
The chromosome is copied, the copies move apart as the cell lengthens, and a septum divides the cell
The nucleus divides by mitosis, the chromosomes condense, and a cell plate divides the cell in two
questions.explanation: Replication begins at one point on the circular chromosome; the two copies attach to the membrane and are separated as the cell grows, then a new wall and membrane (the septum) form between them. There is no nucleus, spindle or halving of the DNA.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares binary fission with mitosis?
options: Binary fission involves no spindle or nuclear envelope; mitosis divides a nucleus using a spindle
Binary fission produces genetically different cells; mitosis produces genetically identical cells
Binary fission occurs only in eukaryotes; mitosis occurs only in bacteria and archaea
Binary fission halves the chromosome number; mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same
questions.explanation: Both processes produce genetically identical cells with a full copy of the DNA. Binary fission is simpler because prokaryotes have one circular chromosome and no nucleus, so no spindle or nuclear envelope is involved.

questions.stem: Under ideal conditions a bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting from one cell, how many cells are present after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: Three hours is 180 minutes, which is 9 generations of 20 minutes, so the number of cells is 2 to the power 9 = 512. 256 is 8 generations, and 18 wrongly doubles the number of generations instead of the cells.

questions.stem: A culture starts with 50 bacteria that divide every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are present after 2 hours, assuming no cells die?
questions.explanation: Two hours is 6 generations, so the number is 50 x 2 to the power 6 = 50 x 64 = 3200. 600 treats growth as linear (50 x 2 x 6), and 6400 counts one generation too many.

questions.stem: All the bacteria in a colony grown from one cell by binary fission are genetically identical except for a few. What is the most likely source of the differences?
options: Fertilisation between bacteria during each cycle of division
Independent assortment of the chromosomes into the daughter cells
Mutations arising from errors when the chromosome was replicated
Crossing over between chromosomes during each binary fission
questions.explanation: Binary fission copies the chromosome, so offspring are clones; occasional replication errors introduce new mutations. Crossing over, independent assortment and fertilisation belong to sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA and increase in number within a cell. How do they reproduce?
options: By being built new from proteins made in the cytosol
By dividing in a process similar to binary fission
By mitosis, using the same spindle as the nucleus
By meiosis, which halves their DNA at each division
questions.explanation: These organelles copy their circular DNA and divide by a fission process like that of bacteria, which is evidence of their bacterial origin. They are not made new from scratch, and they do not use the nuclear spindle.

questions.stem: In which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle is DNA replicated?
options: S phase of interphase
Prophase of mitosis
G2 phase of interphase
Cytokinesis
questions.explanation: DNA synthesis takes place during the S phase of interphase, so that each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids before mitosis begins. G2 follows S and prepares the cell for division.

questions.stem: Most cells in a tissue sample are seen to be in interphase. Why is this expected?
options: Interphase is the longest part of the cell cycle, so most cells are in it at any time
Cells in interphase are not alive, so they collect in large numbers in the tissue
Interphase is when chromosomes are most visible, so these cells are easiest to count
Cells divide only once in their life, so most have finished dividing and stay in it
questions.explanation: The proportion of cells in a phase reflects how long that phase lasts, and interphase, including growth and DNA replication, takes up most of the cycle. Chromosomes are actually least visible in interphase.

questions.stem: A cell has a certain amount of DNA, x, at the start of interphase. How much DNA is in each daughter cell after mitosis and cytokinesis?
options: x
2x
4x
questions.explanation: DNA doubles to 2x during the S phase, then is shared equally between two daughter cells, each receiving x. Mitosis therefore keeps the amount of DNA, and the chromosome number, the same from cell to cell.

questions.stem: In a root tip, 24 of 200 cells examined are undergoing mitosis. What is the mitotic index?
questions.explanation: Mitotic index = cells in mitosis / total cells x 100 = 24 / 200 x 100 = 12%. 88% is the percentage not in mitosis, and 8.3 comes from dividing 200 by 24.

questions.stem: Of 400 cells in an onion root tip, 20 are in metaphase. If one cell cycle takes 20 hours, about how long does metaphase last?
options: 1 hour
5 hours
20 minutes
2 hours
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in a phase estimates the fraction of the cycle spent in it: 20 / 400 = 0.05, and 0.05 x 20 hours = 1 hour. This assumes the cells are dividing independently, not in step.

questions.stem: In which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell?
options: Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
Metaphase
questions.explanation: In metaphase the chromosomes are attached to spindle fibres and align on the cell's equator. They condense in prophase, separate in anaphase and reach the poles in telophase.

questions.stem: Which events take place during prophase of mitosis?
options: Chromosomes condense, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle forms
Sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles of the cell
Chromosomes line up on the equator, each attached to spindle fibres
Nuclear envelopes re-form around two groups of chromosomes at the poles
questions.explanation: Prophase prepares for division: chromosomes coil up and become visible as two chromatids joined at a centromere, the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibres form. Separation of chromatids is anaphase.

questions.stem: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
options: The centromeres split and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
Homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite ends of the cell
The chromosomes uncoil and new nuclear envelopes form around each group
The DNA is copied so that each chromosome has two identical chromatids
questions.explanation: Spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids apart, so each pole receives one copy of every chromosome. Homologous chromosomes separating is anaphase I of meiosis, not mitosis.

questions.stem: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromatids are present at metaphase of mitosis, and how many chromosomes are in the cell during anaphase?
options: 92 chromatids at metaphase; 46 chromosomes in anaphase
46 chromatids at metaphase; 23 chromosomes in anaphase
92 chromatids at metaphase; 92 chromosomes in anaphase
46 chromatids at metaphase; 46 chromosomes in anaphase
questions.explanation: After replication each of the 46 chromosomes has two chromatids, giving 92 at metaphase. In anaphase the chromatids separate and each counts as a chromosome, so 92 are present briefly, 46 moving to each pole.

questions.stem: What is the role of the spindle fibres in mitosis?
options: To pinch the cell membrane inwards to split the cytoplasm in two
To attach to the centromeres and move the chromatids to opposite poles
To copy the DNA so that each chromosome has two identical chromatids
To hold the nuclear envelope together until the chromosomes separate
questions.explanation: Spindle fibres made of microtubules attach at the centromeres, align the chromosomes and then pull sister chromatids apart. DNA is copied in S phase, and the cytoplasm is divided by cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A drug stops spindle fibres from forming. Cells treated with it are found to be stuck at one stage. Which stage, and why?
options: In G1, because the cell cannot grow without spindle fibres to support it
Before anaphase, because the chromatids cannot be moved apart
In S phase, because the spindle is needed to copy the DNA of each chromosome
In cytokinesis, because the spindle is what pinches the cytoplasm in two
questions.explanation: Without a spindle, chromosomes cannot align and their chromatids cannot be separated, so cells halt before anaphase with condensed chromosomes. DNA replication in S phase does not use the spindle.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows a cell with two groups of chromosomes at opposite ends, new nuclear envelopes forming and the chromosomes starting to uncoil. Which stage is this?
options: Prophase
Interphase
Telophase
Metaphase
questions.explanation: Telophase reverses the events of prophase: nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense at each pole. Prophase looks similar but the chromosomes are condensing and the envelope is breaking down.

questions.stem: After mitosis is complete, cytokinesis takes place. What does it involve?
options: Division of the cytoplasm to form two separate cells
Division of the nucleus into two identical nuclei
Copying of the DNA before the cell begins to divide
Condensing of the chromosomes at the start of mitosis
questions.explanation: Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm and organelles, completing the formation of two cells. DNA copying happens earlier, in S phase.

questions.stem: How does cytokinesis differ between animal and plant cells?
options: Animal cells do not carry out cytokinesis; plant cells divide only their cytoplasm
Animal cells divide by binary fission; plant cells divide by mitosis and cytokinesis
Animal cells form a cleavage furrow; plant cells build a cell plate that becomes a new wall
Animal cells build a cell plate; plant cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches inwards
questions.explanation: In animal cells a ring of protein filaments pinches the membrane inwards. A rigid plant cell wall cannot pinch, so vesicles gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate, which develops into a new wall.

questions.stem: Which process uses mitosis?
options: Reproduction of a bacterial cell
Repairing damaged skin tissue
Producing sperm cells in the testes
Joining an egg and a sperm cell
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Sperm are made by meiosis, joining gametes is fertilisation, and bacteria divide by binary fission.

questions.stem: A strawberry plant sends out runners that grow into new plants. How do the new plants compare genetically with the parent, and why?
options: They are identical, because their cells were produced by meiosis
They differ, because each runner is formed by fertilisation
They are identical, because their cells were produced by mitosis
They differ, because their cells were produced by meiosis
questions.explanation: Runners are a form of asexual reproduction: their cells come from the parent by mitosis, so the new plants are clones. Meiosis and fertilisation produce genetic variation in sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: How does mitosis contribute to the growth of a multicellular organism from a zygote?
options: It increases the number of cells, each with the same genetic information as the zygote
It increases the size of each cell without changing the number of cells in the body
It halves the chromosome number so that different tissues can form in the body
It shuffles the alleles in each new cell so that different cell types can form
questions.explanation: Repeated mitotic divisions produce the trillions of cells of an adult, all with the zygote's genetic information. Different cell types arise from differential gene expression, not from changes to the DNA.

questions.stem: Why do mutations in genes that control the cell cycle sometimes lead to cancer?
options: Cells may divide repeatedly without the normal checks, forming a tumour
Cells stop dividing altogether, so damaged tissue can no longer be repaired
Cells switch from mitosis to meiosis, so they produce gametes in the tissue
Cells lose their DNA during division, so they can no longer make proteins
questions.explanation: Checkpoints normally stop a cell dividing if its DNA is damaged or conditions are wrong. If the genes controlling these checks mutate, cells can divide uncontrollably and form a mass called a tumour.

questions.stem: Which statement about the products of one mitotic division of a diploid cell is correct?
options: Two diploid cells, genetically identical to each other and to the parent
Four haploid cells, each genetically different from the parent cell
Two haploid cells, each with one chromosome from every homologous pair
Four diploid cells, genetically identical to each other and to the parent
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number and genes as the parent. Four genetically different haploid cells are the products of meiosis.

questions.stem: Students make a squash of an onion root tip to observe mitosis. Why is the root tip used rather than a mature leaf?
options: Root tips contain no chromosomes, so the spindle is easier to see
Leaf cells divide by binary fission, so mitosis cannot be seen
Leaf cells have no nucleus, so their chromosomes cannot be stained
Root tips contain a growing region where many cells are dividing
questions.explanation: The tip of a growing root has a meristem where cells divide frequently, so many cells are caught in stages of mitosis. Mature leaf cells have mostly stopped dividing, though they do have nuclei and chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which feature of a dividing cell shows it is undergoing mitosis rather than meiosis?
options: Each daughter nucleus receives only one chromosome from each pair
Chromosomes line up singly, not in homologous pairs, at metaphase
Homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over during the prophase stage
The cell divides twice in a row, producing four nuclei from one nucleus
questions.explanation: In mitosis each chromosome lines up independently on the equator and its sister chromatids separate. Pairing of homologues, crossing over, two divisions and halving the chromosome number are features of meiosis.

questions.stem: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative. What does this mean?
options: Half of the genes are copied, and the other half are kept by the parent
One new DNA molecule keeps both original strands; the other has two new
Each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one newly made strand
Each new DNA molecule is made entirely of newly made nucleotide strands
questions.explanation: The two strands separate and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so every new molecule keeps one original strand. This is why the copies passed to daughter cells are identical.

questions.stem: What is a chromatid?
options: One strand of the DNA double helix, separated from its partner in replication
A spindle fibre that attaches to a chromosome's centromere at metaphase
One of two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere
One of a pair of homologous chromosomes, one inherited from each parent
questions.explanation: After S phase each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids held together at the centromere; they separate in anaphase. Homologous chromosomes are a different pair, carrying the same genes but possibly different alleles.

questions.stem: What mainly happens during the G1 phase of interphase?
options: The DNA is replicated to form sister chromatids
The chromosomes condense and the spindle forms
The cytoplasm divides to form two separate cells
The cell grows and makes proteins and organelles
questions.explanation: G1 is a period of growth and normal cell activity before DNA is copied in S phase. Chromosome condensation is part of prophase, and division of the cytoplasm is cytokinesis.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the stages of mitosis in the correct order?
options: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Metaphase, prophase, telophase, anaphase
Prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase
Anaphase, metaphase, prophase, telophase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense in prophase, line up in metaphase, separate in anaphase and reach the poles in telophase. Cytokinesis usually begins during telophase and completes the division.

questions.stem: A dog body cell contains 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell after the cell divides by mitosis?
questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant, so each daughter cell has the same 78 chromosomes as the parent. 39 is the number in a dog gamete made by meiosis, and 156 forgets that the copies are shared between two cells.

questions.stem: A bacterium carries a plasmid with a gene for antibiotic resistance. Why are both daughter cells usually resistant after binary fission?
options: The plasmid is copied before division, so copies pass to both daughter cells
The plasmid splits in half at division, and each half carries the gene
Each daughter cell builds a new resistance gene from proteins in the cytoplasm
Only one daughter cell receives the plasmid, then passes it on by fertilisation
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small circles of DNA that replicate independently of the main chromosome, and the copies are shared between the daughter cells. Bacteria do not reproduce by fertilisation.

questions.stem: A crop is grown entirely from cuttings, a form of asexual reproduction by mitosis. What is the main risk if a new plant disease arrives?
options: The plants reproduce more slowly than seedlings, so the crop cannot recover
The plants inherit no genes from the parent, so they have no resistance genes
The plants are genetically identical, so if one is susceptible they all are
The plants have half the parent's chromosomes, so they are weaker than seedlings
questions.explanation: Mitosis copies the parent's genes exactly, so a clone lacks the variation that might include resistant individuals. Asexual reproduction is usually faster than sexual reproduction, and the cuttings carry the full chromosome number.

questions.stem: A graph shows the DNA content of one cell over time. The DNA doubles gradually over several hours, stays constant for a while, then halves suddenly. What do the gradual rise and the sudden fall represent?
options: The rise is mitosis; the fall is S phase, when the extra DNA is broken down
The rise is G1 growth; the fall is anaphase, when half the DNA is destroyed
The rise is cytokinesis; the fall is prophase, when chromosomes condense
The rise is S phase; the fall is when the cell divides into two cells
questions.explanation: DNA is synthesised steadily during S phase, then stays at double the amount through G2 and mitosis. When the cell divides, each daughter cell receives half, restoring the original amount. No DNA is destroyed.

questions.stem: During anaphase of mitosis, one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate and both move to the same pole. What is the result for the two daughter cells?
options: Both cells are haploid, because the chromosome number has halved
Both cells have an extra chromosome, because the DNA was copied twice
One cell has an extra chromosome and the other is missing one
Both cells have the normal number, but each carries a gene mutation
questions.explanation: If both chromatids go to one pole, that daughter cell gains a chromosome and the other lacks it. This is a chromosome mutation caused by an error in cell division, not an error in DNA replication.
